title: Goodnight Stories | The Nightingale and the Rose (A Retelling)
subtitle: She loves her, she loves her, she loves her—huh? How is it that in this world, no one loves each other anymore? Why is everyone unhappy? Why does everyone love someone else, but not themselves? — Hebe Tien, “LOVE”
body:
Once there was a girl who fell in love with the professor’s daughter, a girl in a year above her. The older girl said that if she could bring her a red rose at Christmas, she would dance with her. But roses did not bloom in winter. The girl was terribly sad and tossed and turned at night, unable to sleep. The nightingale outside her window heard her crying. The nightingale very much wanted to help this poor child. She flew and flew until she found a rosebush. The rosebush told her: only if she pressed her breast against its thorn and sang all night could it use her blood to nourish a red rose. The nightingale thought about it. She truly loved this girl, and decided to exchange herself for the girl’s chance to be with the person she liked. So she pressed herself against the rose’s thorn and sang all night, until the sky turned fish-belly white. When she had sung her last note and could sing no more, the rosebush finally produced an exquisitely beautiful red rose.
The girl opened her window, saw the rose, and cried out in delighted surprise. She carefully cut it, wrapped it in pretty floral paper, and hurried excitedly to the professor’s garden, only to see the older girl laughing and playing with a boy. Timidly, the girl called out to her and offered the rose. The older girl raised her eyebrows. “It must have been quite a struggle to find such a beautiful rose in the depths of winter.” The girl looked expectantly into her eyes. “Then, the dance?” The older girl smiled gently: “Silly. I’m afraid I’ll have to disappoint you this time.” “She’s already agreed to be my dance partner. Sorry, little junior.” The older boy beside her bent down with a smug smile.
The girl felt her stomach heaving upward while her heart sank. Suddenly she remembered that the nightingale who sang by her bed every day seemed not to have come that morning. Unease suddenly stirred in her. She asked for the rose back, intending to give it to the nightingale. She thought: it was not quite repayment, but she simply felt that a rose this lovely should not be wasted on the wrong person.
But when she ran home, she found that the nightingale had fallen into a deep sleep beneath the rose branch outside her window, and would never wake again. The girl understood everything at once. Staggering, she knelt beside the nightingale and, choking with sobs, buried the rose and the nightingale in the earth.
The girl wept all night. When the first ray of sunlight touched her face the next morning, she faintly heard clear birdsong outside the window. It seemed to be her nightingale’s voice, yet seemed too young. The girl clung to this dream, afraid to wake. Yet she could not resist opening the window. To her surprise, all the roses had bloomed overnight. Perched on a branch was a fluffy little nightingale, so like the nightingale before! Her features, and the way she looked at the girl, were alike.
The girl plucked a rose petal and offered it to the little nightingale. “I’ve only just realized: you’re the one I most wanted to give a rose to.”
